title: Fatigue Failure: From Small Cracks to Sudden Fracture

scenes.title: Fatigue Failure
scenes.speech: Fatigue failure: from small cracks to sudden fracture. First, we explain the science. Then, we apply it to a bicycle crank.

scenes.title: Repeated loads can cause failure
scenes.speech: Metals can fail under repeated loading, even when stress stays below yield strength. One safe-looking load does not mean thousands of repeated loads are safe.

scenes.title: A crack needs a starting point
scenes.speech: This real titanium specimen shows a crack starting at a defect. Scratches, holes, and sharp corners can also concentrate stress.

scenes.title: Slow damage. A sudden final break.
scenes.speech: First, a small crack starts. Repeated loads can then extend it. As the crack grows, less intact metal carries the load. Finally, the remaining section breaks rapidly. Damage builds gradually; the last break looks sudden.

scenes.title: Read an S-N curve
scenes.speech: An S-N curve connects stress amplitude with cycles to failure. Amplitude is half the stress range. The horizontal axis is logarithmic: each step means ten times more cycles.

scenes.title: Higher amplitude, shorter life
scenes.speech: Follow three hundred megapascals across to the curve, then down: ten thousand cycles. At one hundred eighty megapascals, read one million cycles. Lower amplitude gives longer life under the same conditions.

scenes.title: A trend, with real-world variation
scenes.speech: These numbers are illustrative, not crank measurements. Real test results scatter. Some steels show a fatigue limit; aluminum alloys generally have no clear limit.

scenes.title: Loading versus resistance
scenes.speech: Fracture toughness means resistance to fracture from an existing crack. K one describes crack-tip loading. K one C is the material's plane-strain fracture toughness under valid conditions.

scenes.title: What controls stress intensity?
scenes.speech: Here, Y is a geometry factor, sigma is stress, and a is crack length. This formula estimates the stress intensity factor.

scenes.title: Two ways to increase K_I
scenes.speech: Keep crack length fixed and increase stress: K one rises. Keep stress fixed and lengthen the crack: K one usually rises.

scenes.title: Growth can begin before rapid fracture
scenes.speech: With linear elasticity and plane strain, rapid fracture may occur when maximum K one reaches K one C. Fatigue cracks can still grow below this critical value.

scenes.title: Why can a bicycle crank suddenly break?
scenes.speech: Why can a bicycle crank suddenly break after repeated pedaling? This arm transfers pedal force to the drivetrain.

scenes.title: Each pedal stroke changes the load
scenes.speech: Each stroke changes the load. Pedal threads, axle connections, scratches, and sharp corners can concentrate stress.

scenes.title: The final break hides a longer history
scenes.speech: This real broken crank shows fatigue growth and final fracture. A small crack can grow over many uses.

scenes.title: Connect the three ideas
scenes.speech: Higher amplitude usually shortens fatigue life. Longer cracks raise stress intensity, making rapid fracture possible.

scenes.title: Protect. Notice. Inspect.
scenes.speech: Protect surfaces, notice changes, and check for cracks. Stop using a suspect part. References and photo credits are provided.
